teile.einleitung: In a mine, people dig mineral resources out of the earth, for example ore, coal or salt. The work is often deep underground. Miners have their own words, customs and even their own greeting.
wichtigste: Mineral resources are extracted in a mine.
Someone who works in a mine is called a miner.
A tunnel called an adit runs horizontally, while a shaft runs vertically.
In the past, canaries warned of poisonous gas.
The German miners' greeting is “Glück auf”.
Iron ore was mined for a long time in the Gonzen near Sargans.

abschnitte.text: A **mine** is a place where **mineral resources** are taken from the earth. These can be ores, from which metals are obtained, or coal and salt. Sometimes the raw materials lie close to the surface. But often you have to dig deep into the ground. Miners call working below the ground working **underground**.

An **adit** is an almost horizontal tunnel into the mountain. You can walk into it or ride in on small trains. A **shaft**, on the other hand, leads **vertically** down into the depths. **Cages** carrying people and material travel up and down it. Because it is pitch dark underground, miners wear a **lamp on their helmet**.

Working in a mine used to be very dangerous. Tunnels could collapse, and water could get in. Especially feared was **poisonous gas** that you cannot smell. That is why miners took **canaries** with them. These react quickly to the gas. If the bird became weak, the miners knew they had to get out at once. Today electronic devices measure the air.

German-speaking miners traditionally greet each other with **“Glück auf”**, which means something like “good luck up there”. The greeting wishes that you come back up to the surface safe and sound. Many miners honour **St Barbara** as their patron saint. Her feast day is **4 December**. In some areas miners hold special celebrations on this day.

There were mines in Switzerland too. In the **Gonzen** near **Sargans** in the canton of St Gallen, **iron ore** was mined for a long time. Today the mine is closed, and you can visit it. In **Bex** in the canton of Vaud, salt has been produced for centuries, and there are guided tours through the tunnels there too.

gewusst: The miners' greeting “Glück auf” is still used today, including in songs.
The canaries in the mine were a kind of living gas detector.

teile.einleitung: A rock glacier looks like a huge heap of stones slowly creeping down a slope. But under the blocks of stone there is a lot of ice. Rock glaciers are only found where the ground is permanently frozen.
wichtigste: A rock glacier consists of rock debris with ice in between.
Active rock glaciers need permafrost.
They creep about 10 centimetres to 1 metre a year.
The share of ice beneath the layer of boulders is often 40 to 70 per cent.
Fossil rock glaciers show that it used to be colder.
Rock glaciers are studied particularly closely in the Engadine.

abschnitte.text: A **rock glacier** is a mixture of **rock debris and ice**. It creeps slowly down the slope like a thick porridge. The surface is made of coarse boulders. Underneath, it often contains **40 to 70 per cent ice**, sometimes even more. Because you cannot see the ice, a rock glacier looks like an ordinary **scree slope** to non-experts.

The ice in a rock glacier only survives if the ground is **permanently frozen**. Such ground is called **permafrost**. In the Swiss Alps, permafrost is found mainly at high altitudes and on shady slopes. That is why rock glaciers are seen as typical signs of permafrost. They often have a steep front and wavy ridges on the surface.

Active rock glaciers typically move **0.1 to 1 metre a year**. That is much slower than most ice glaciers. If the permafrost gets warmer, some rock glaciers can speed up. That is why experts watch them closely. If stones come loose at the front, this can be dangerous for paths and buildings below.

Some rock glaciers today contain **no more ice** and do not move. They are called **fossil**. Today they lie outside the permafrost zone. But their shape shows that there used to be permafrost there and therefore a **colder climate**. In this way they help us to understand the history of the climate.

In the **Engadine**, rock glaciers are studied particularly closely, for example the **Murtèl-Corvatsch** rock glacier. Researchers drilled down to the bottom there and installed measuring instruments. In this way they have been measuring temperature and movement for many years. In 2022 the Engadine rock glaciers were put on a list of 100 important geological heritage sites in the world.

gewusst: From the outside you usually cannot see the ice of a rock glacier at all.
The measurements at Murtèl-Corvatsch are among the longest series of permafrost measurements in the Alps.

teile.einleitung: Bowen's reaction series describes the order in which minerals crystallise out of a cooling rock melt. It is named after the Canadian geologist Norman L. Bowen. It helps to explain why such different rocks as basalt and granite can form from similar melts.
wichtigste: Olivine is the first mineral to crystallise from a basalt melt.
The discontinuous series leads via pyroxene, amphibole and biotite.
The continuous branch is formed by the plagioclases.
As it cools, plagioclase changes from calcium-rich to sodium-rich.
At the end, potassium feldspar, muscovite and finally quartz crystallise.
Fractional crystallisation makes the remaining melt richer in SiO₂.
Basalt melts begin to crystallise at about 1200 °C.

abschnitte.text: A **magma** is a rock melt deep inside the Earth. When it cools, not all minerals form at the same time. Each mineral crystallises in a certain **temperature range**. Basaltic melts start to crystallise at about **1200 °C**. Granitic remaining melts, on the other hand, only harden at about 650 to 700 °C. **Norman L. Bowen** studied this sequence at the beginning of the 20th century with laboratory experiments.

In the **discontinuous branch**, different minerals, each with a different crystal structure, follow one another. First **olivine** forms, then **pyroxene**, after that **amphibole** and **biotite**. At each step the **silicate tetrahedra** are more strongly linked to each other. Crystals formed early are no longer stable as the temperature falls. If they stay in contact with the remaining melt, they **react** to form a new mineral. That is where the name reaction series comes from.

Alongside this runs the **continuous branch** of the **plagioclases**. Here the crystal structure stays the same; only the chemical make-up of the **solid solution** changes. At high temperature, calcium-rich **anorthite** crystallises. As the temperature falls, the plagioclase becomes more and more sodium-rich, all the way to **albite**. In between there are seamless transitions.

At the end a **remaining melt** is left that is rich in SiO₂, potassium and water. From it, **potassium feldspar** and **muscovite** crystallise. The last mineral to form is **quartz**, pure silicon dioxide. These minerals are typical of **granite**. That is why there is hardly any quartz in basalt, but a great deal in granite.

When heavy crystals formed early sink to the bottom of the magma chamber, they are separated from the melt. They can then no longer react with it. This process is called **fractional crystallisation**. As a result, the melt changes its make-up step by step and becomes **richer in SiO₂**. In this way a basaltic starting melt can gradually turn into a much lighter-coloured melt.

gewusst: Minerals from the start of the series, such as olivine, usually weather faster at the Earth's surface than quartz from the end of the series.
Bowen published his results in 1928 in the book “The Evolution of the Igneous Rocks”.

teile.einleitung: An ice-dammed lake is a lake held back by a glacier, as if by a dam. Such lakes can suddenly drain and cause floods. A well-known example in Switzerland is the Märjelensee on the Great Aletsch Glacier.
wichtigste: An ice-dammed lake forms when glacier ice blocks a valley and water collects behind it.
It can suddenly burst out and cause a flood.
The Märjelensee lies on the eastern edge of the Great Aletsch Glacier.
In the 19th century, a lot of water flowed through the Massa gorge during outbursts.
In 1895 a relief tunnel was built against the outbursts.
A sudden outburst of a glacier lake is called by an Icelandic word, jökulhlaup.

abschnitte.text: A glacier can block a **side valley** like a dam. Behind it, meltwater and rainwater collect into an **ice-dammed lake**. But ice is not a solid wall. The water can find its way through cracks or under the ice. Then the lake often drains in a short time and causes a **flood** further down.

The **Märjelensee** lies in a hollow on the eastern edge of the **Great Aletsch Glacier** in Valais. In the 19th century the glacier was much thicker, and the lake was up to 1.6 kilometres long. During outbursts the water drained through crevasses in the glacier and caused floods in the **Massa**, which flows from the Aletsch Glacier to the Rhône. In 1895 a **relief tunnel** over 500 metres long was built, which limited how high the lake could rise.

Since the 19th century the Aletsch Glacier has **shrunk** a great deal. Today it is much thinner and holds back less water. So the natural Märjelensee is hardly 100 metres long any more and drains almost every year. Because the glacier retreated, the tunnel was only rarely needed. The lake shows clearly how much the glaciers of the Alps have changed.

abschnitte.titel: Huge lakes of the Ice Age
abschnitte.text: In **Iceland**, dammed glacier lakes often burst out. The Icelandic word **jökulhlaup** means something like “glacier run”. After the last cold period, a huge lake was dammed up at the edge of the North American ice sheet. It was named after the Swiss naturalist **Louis Agassiz** and is called **Lake Agassiz**. It was bigger than any lake on Earth today.

gewusst: Louis Agassiz came from the canton of Fribourg and later became a famous scientist in the USA.
Today glacier lakes in Switzerland are monitored by experts so that people can be warned in time before an outburst.

teile.einleitung: The Burgess Shale is a famous fossil site in the Canadian Rocky Mountains. It preserves animals from the Cambrian that lived in the sea about 508 million years ago. What is special is that even their soft body parts have been preserved.
wichtigste: The Burgess Shale is in Yoho National Park in British Columbia, Canada.
Charles Walcott discovered the site in 1909.
The fossils are about 508 million years old and come from the middle Cambrian.
Even soft parts such as muscles, gills and guts were preserved.
Well-known animals are Opabinia, Hallucigenia and Pikaia.
Stephen Jay Gould made the site world famous with “Wonderful Life”.

abschnitte.text: The **Burgess Shale** is in **Yoho National Park** in the Canadian province of British Columbia. It is part of the Canadian Rocky Mountain Parks UNESCO World Heritage Site. It was discovered in **1909** by the American palaeontologist **Charles Doolittle Walcott**. At that time Walcott was head of the Smithsonian Institution in Washington. In the following years he collected tens of thousands of fossils from the shale.

The fossils are about **508 million years** old. They come from the **middle Cambrian**. At that time many new groups of animals appeared in the sea. The Burgess Shale is a little younger than the early Cambrian fauna of **Chengjiang** in China, which is also very well preserved.

Usually only the hard parts of animals, such as shells or bones, are left as fossils. In the Burgess Shale it is different. **Mudflows** buried the animals quickly and **cut off from the air**. That is why even **muscles, gills and guts**, which usually rot away, were preserved. So researchers know what animals that had no hard parts looked like.

**Opabinia** had **five eyes** and a trunk with a grasping claw. When its reconstruction was first presented, the audience laughed, it seemed so strange. Today it is seen as a relative of the early arthropods. **Hallucigenia** was first reconstructed upside down: people thought the spines were legs and the legs were tentacles on its back. Today it is seen as a relative of the **velvet worms**.

**Pikaia** had a rod along its back, the so-called **notochord**, and muscular body segments. It is seen as an early **chordate** and therefore as a distant relative of the vertebrates. In 1989 the palaeontologist **Stephen Jay Gould** made the Burgess Shale world famous with the book **“Wonderful Life”**. He interpreted the strange animals as a sign of how strongly **chance** shapes evolution. In German the book appeared as “Zufall Mensch”, meaning “Humans by chance”.

gewusst: The name Hallucigenia is a reminder of how dreamlike and strange this animal seemed to the researchers.
Tens of thousands of fossils have been collected from the Burgess Shale.

teile.einleitung: On 18 October 1356 a severe earthquake shook the city of Basel. Afterwards the city burned for days. It is the strongest earthquake recorded in the history of Central Europe.
wichtigste: The main earthquake happened on the afternoon of 18 October 1356.
A fire that lasted for days destroyed many wooden houses.
The epicentre was probably a few kilometres south of Basel near Reinach BL.
The choir of Basel Minster collapsed.
Over a wide area, about 40 castles were damaged or destroyed.
The magnitude is estimated at about 6 to 7, with 6.6 often given.
It is the strongest historically documented earthquake in Central Europe.

abschnitte.text: The Basel earthquake happened on **18 October 1356**, the feast day of St Luke the Evangelist. A **foreshock** had already frightened people before that. So many left the city. The main earthquake followed in the afternoon. That is probably why fewer people died than you might expect. The figures for the number of dead vary greatly, between about 100 and 2000.

At that time many houses in Basel were made of **wood**. The earthquake knocked over hearth fires and lamps. The flames spread quickly. According to the old sources, the **city fire** raged for eight days. It destroyed a large part of the city.

At **Basel Minster**, the **choir** collapsed and the roof fell into the nave. Altars, the organ and pictures were destroyed. There was also great damage over a wide area. About **40 castles** were badly hit. Many were rebuilt later, while others remained ruins. On the corner tower of the former city wall near the **Lohnhof**, earthquake damage can still be seen today.

According to today's research, the source of the earthquake was a few kilometres south of Basel near **Reinach BL**. A deep **fault zone** runs through the Earth's crust there. There were no measuring instruments in the Middle Ages. So experts estimate the strength from the damage that was recorded. The values lie between about 6 and 7 on the **magnitude scale**, with 6.6 often given.

No other recorded earthquake in Central Europe was as strong. That is why the Basel earthquake serves as an important **yardstick** for the earthquake risk in the region. Experts know that a similar earthquake could happen again today. That is why there are rules in Switzerland for **earthquake-proof building**. The Basel region is one of the areas with a higher earthquake risk.

gewusst: The earthquake was so strong that it could still be felt clearly far away.
More than 650 years have passed since the Basel earthquake.

teile.einleitung: Pumice is a very special stone: it is so light that it floats on water. It forms during volcanic eruptions from frothed-up lava. Many people know it from the bathroom.
wichtigste: Pumice floats on water.
It is full of small holes filled with air.
Pumice forms when lava froths up because of gas bubbles.
It is usually light grey, white or beige.
Its surface feels rough.
It is used for foot care, for light building blocks and in the past for jeans.

abschnitte.text: Many **gases** are dissolved in the lava of a volcano. In a violent eruption they are suddenly released, rather like when you open a bottle of fizzy water. The lava **froths up**. It cools so quickly that the bubbles stay trapped. This is how **pumice** forms, a volcanic rock full of small holes.

Because pumice has so many air-filled holes, it is very light. It is even lighter than water and therefore **floats**. After some eruptions under water, huge **rafts of pumice** drift on the sea. They can cover hundreds of square kilometres. Over time the stones soak up water and sink.

Pumice is usually **light-coloured**, often light grey, white or beige. That makes it different from dark lava rocks such as basalt. Because of the many holes, the surface has tiny sharp edges. That is why pumice feels **rough**, almost like sandpaper.

In the bathroom, many people use pumice to gently rub away **hard skin** on their feet. On building sites it is used to make **light building blocks** and mortar. In the past some **jeans** were washed together with pumice stones in large machines. The rough stones rubbed off the colour, and the trousers looked faded. This was called **stonewashed**.

gewusst: Pumice is one of the few stones that float on water.
After eruptions, drifting rafts of pumice can travel long distances across the sea.

teile.einleitung: A mountain is a rise in the land that is clearly higher than its surroundings. In Switzerland you can see mountains everywhere, from the gentle Jura to the mighty Alps with their glaciers. Mountains form over millions of years, when parts of the Earth's crust are pushed together and lifted up.
wichtigste: A mountain is a rise in the land that is clearly higher than its surroundings.
The highest point of a mountain is called the summit.
The Alps are Switzerland's large mountain range with very high mountains.
The Jura mountains lie in the north-west of Switzerland.
The Matterhorn is world famous for its pointed shape.
The higher you climb, the colder it usually gets.
The highest mountain in Switzerland is the Dufourspitze in the Monte Rosa massif, at 4634 metres.

abschnitte.text: A **mountain** rises clearly above its surroundings. Its highest point is called the **summit**, and its sides are called slopes or flanks. Several mountains together form a **mountain range**. A saddle between two peaks that you can cross is called a pass. The height of a mountain is measured in metres above sea level.

Most large mountain ranges form when two **tectonic plates** collide. The Earth's crust is pushed together, folded and lifted. This is how the Alps formed, when the African Plate pushed against the Eurasian Plate. This process took many millions of years and is not quite finished yet. Other mountains are **volcanoes**, built up from lava that has flowed out. At the same time, wind, water and glaciers slowly wear the mountains down again.

The **Alps** cover about 60 per cent of Switzerland. There are 48 peaks here that are over 4000 metres high. The highest mountain in Switzerland is the Dufourspitze at 4634 metres, and the most famous landmark is the **Matterhorn** near Zermatt with its pointed shape. In the north-west lies the **Jura**, a lower range of folded mountains with long, wooded ridges. Its highest Swiss peak is Mont Tendre at 1679 metres.

The higher you climb, the **colder** it gets: on average by about 0.6 °C per 100 metres. That is why there is snow on high peaks even in summer. It is also why the plants change with height: lower down there are broadleaved woods, higher up coniferous forests. At about 2000 metres the forest stops; this is the **tree line**. Above it there are Alpine pastures, rock, snow and glaciers.

Animals live in the mountains that are adapted to the cold and to steep ground. They include the **ibex**, the chamois, the marmot and the golden eagle. People have used the mountains for centuries for **Alpine farming**: in summer cows graze on the high pastures, and the milk is made into cheese. Today the mountains are also important for tourism, skiing and hiking. Many reservoirs in the Alps produce electricity from water power.

Mountain hiking is fun but needs preparation. The weather in the mountains can change quickly, and thunderstorms and fog are dangerous. Good shoes, warm clothes, rain protection and enough to drink belong in your rucksack. In Switzerland, paths are marked with colours: yellow for hiking paths, **white-red-white** for mountain paths and white-blue-white for Alpine routes. In an emergency the air rescue service **Rega** helps on the number 1414.

begriffe.erklaerung: The highest point of a mountain.
A large group of connected mountains.
The height above which no forests can grow.
A lower crossing between two mountains, over which paths or roads lead.

gewusst: The rocks on the summit of the Matterhorn originally came from the African Plate.
The Alps are still being lifted by about a millimetre every year.
On many limestone peaks in the Alps you can find fossilised sea creatures, because these rocks once formed on the sea floor.

teile.einleitung: A drought is a long period when there is far too little rain. Soil, plants, streams and lakes dry out. In Switzerland, too, there have been several drought summers in recent decades, for example in 2003 and 2018.
wichtigste: In a drought there is too little rain for weeks or months.
The soil dries out, shrinks and gets deep cracks.
Crops in the fields dry up, and the harvest is small.
The water level in rivers and lakes falls.
When it is very dry, fires in the forest are often banned.
In the summer of 2018 the army flew water to cows on Swiss Alpine pastures.

abschnitte.text: A **drought** happens when there is much less rain than normal for a long time. Often it is also hot, and the Sun makes even more water evaporate. The soil dries out and shrinks. This creates deep **cracks**. Because less water flows out of the soil, the water level in streams, rivers and lakes also falls.

Plants need water to live. Without rain they wilt, and the **harvest** is small. Farmers then have to water their fields or buy in feed for their animals. Fish suffer too: shallow, warm water contains less **oxygen**. But trout and grayling need cool water. In the hot summer of 2018, many grayling died in the Rhine near Schaffhausen.

Dry leaves, grass and wood burn very easily. Even a small spark can start a big **forest fire**. That is why cantons and municipalities often issue a **fire ban** in and near forests when it is very dry. Sometimes fireworks on 1 August are then banned as well. These rules apply to everyone and protect people and nature.

abschnitte.titel: The drought summer of 2018 in Switzerland
abschnitte.text: In the summer of 2018 there was very little rain in Switzerland for months. On some **Alpine pastures** the springs dried up. So the **Swiss Army** flew water up by helicopter so that the cows had enough to drink. Experts expect such dry summers to become more frequent because of **climate change**.

Everyone can help to save water when it is dry. In the garden you can collect **rainwater** in a water butt and use it for watering. If you water in the evening, you lose less water through evaporation. A layer of grass cuttings or leaves on the flower beds keeps the soil moist for longer.

gewusst: In the hot summer of 2003 it was also extremely dry and hot in Switzerland.
Dried-out soils cannot soak up rain well at first, so during a thunderstorm afterwards a lot of water runs off over the surface.

teile.einleitung: An ice core is a long column of ice that researchers drill out of an ice sheet. Air bubbles, dust and traces of earlier times are trapped in the ice. In this way the ice becomes an archive of the climate going back hundreds of thousands of years.
wichtigste: The EPICA ice core at Dome C in Antarctica goes back about 800,000 years.
At the beginning of 2025 the project “Beyond EPICA” drilled ice that is at least about 1.2 million years old.
The ratio of heavy and light isotopes in the ice reveals the temperature of the past.
In cold periods the CO2 content of the air was about 180 ppm.
Layers with a lot of sulphate show large volcanic eruptions of the past.
Researchers at the University of Bern are leaders in measuring the gases in ice.

abschnitte.text: In Greenland and Antarctica, snow falls every year that no longer melts. Layer by layer it is pressed together, first into **firn** and finally into ice. Small **air bubbles** are trapped in the process. With special drills, researchers bring up long columns of ice, the **ice cores**. The deeper the ice lies, the older it is.

The **temperature** of the past can be worked out from the ice itself. In a colder climate, snow contains fewer heavy **isotopes** of oxygen and hydrogen. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different weights. The air bubbles show how much **CO2** and methane there was in the air in the past. However, the air is younger than the ice around it, because the firn only becomes airtight at a depth of about 50 to 120 metres.

The core from the Russian station **Vostok**, published in 1999, covered about 420,000 years. The core from the European project **EPICA** at Dome C goes back about 800,000 years and shows eight cycles of cold and warm periods. At the beginning of 2025, the project **Beyond EPICA** reached the bedrock at a depth of about 2800 metres at the site Little Dome C. The ice is at least about 1.2 million years old.

The Swiss physicist **Hans Oeschger** from the University of Bern was a pioneer of ice core research. Sudden jumps in climate during the last cold period are named after him and the Dane **Willi Dansgaard**: the **Dansgaard-Oeschger events**. Researchers in Bern also measured the greenhouse gases in the EPICA core. They showed that CO2 and temperature are closely linked: in cold periods the CO2 content was about **180 ppm**, in warm periods much higher.

Large **volcanic eruptions** fling sulphur gases into the air. These fall to the ground as **sulphate** with the snow. In the ice core they can be recognised as layers with a higher sulphate content. Such peaks also help to match up the dates of cores from Greenland and Antarctica.

gewusst: The abbreviation ppm means “parts per million”, so 180 ppm means 180 CO2 particles in a million particles of air.
Today the CO2 content of the air is over 400 ppm, higher than at any time in the known ice cores.

teile.einleitung: Gemstones are rare, beautiful and hard minerals. When cut, they sparkle in the light and are used for jewellery and crowns. Well-known gemstones are ruby, sapphire, emerald and diamond.
wichtigste: The ruby is red; its name comes from the Latin word for red.
The emerald is bright green.
Most sapphires are blue.
The amethyst is purple and a form of quartz.
Gemstones are valuable because they are rare, beautiful and hard.
Cutting gives them many smooth faces, and they sparkle.

abschnitte.text: Gemstones are **minerals** that form in the earth. They are particularly **rare**, beautifully coloured and **hard**. Because they are so hard, they hardly get scratched and stay beautiful for a long time. The hardest natural substance is **diamond**. On the Mohs hardness scale it has the highest value, 10.

The **ruby** is red, and its name comes from the Latin word “ruber” for red. The **sapphire** is usually blue, but there are also other colours. Ruby and sapphire are actually the same mineral, **corundum**. Only tiny added substances give them their colour. The **emerald** is bright green and is one of the most valuable gemstones. The **amethyst** is purple and a form of quartz.

In their raw state, gemstones often look plain. Only the **gem cutter** makes them shine. He grinds many small, smooth faces into the stone. These faces are called **facets**. The light is bent and reflected by them. This makes the stone sparkle and glitter with every movement.

Gemstones are used mainly for **jewellery**, such as rings, necklaces and earrings. The **crowns** of queens and kings are often set with many gemstones. They were meant to show power and wealth. Some gemstones are so famous that they even have their own name.

Beautiful crystals can also be found in the Swiss Alps. Particularly well known is the clear **rock crystal**, a form of quartz. People who search for crystals in the mountains are called **“Strahler”**. They often climb steep rock faces to find crystal fissures.

gewusst: Diamonds are made only of carbon, just like the graphite in a pencil.
The emerald is a green form of the mineral beryl.

teile.einleitung: In winter, icicles hang from the edges of roofs, fountains and rock faces. They form when dripping water gradually freezes. However beautiful they look, large icicles can also be dangerous.
wichtigste: An icicle forms when dripping water freezes drop by drop.
They grow best when the Sun melts snow but the air is cold.
Because of gravity, icicles grow downwards.
They are pointed at the bottom because the least water reaches there.
When it thaws, they drip and melt.
Large icicles can fall down and injure people.

abschnitte.text: On a sunny winter's day, some snow on the roof melts. The **meltwater** runs to the edge of the roof and drips down. In the cold air, part of it freezes into ice. Drop by drop, new ice is added, and the **icicle** gets longer and longer. Because the water drips downwards due to **gravity**, icicles grow from the top down.

The water flows down the outside of the icicle as a thin film. Much of it freezes on the way. Only a little water reaches the **tip**. That is why the icicle stays thin at the bottom and keeps getting thicker at the top. This creates the typical shape, which looks like an upside-down pyramid or a pointed cone.

Large icicles are heavy and sharp. When it gets warmer or the Sun shines on them, they can suddenly come loose and **fall down**. That is why you should not walk directly under large icicles. House owners sometimes have to have dangerous icicles removed. When it **thaws**, that is, above 0 degrees, icicles drip and get smaller until they fall off.

There are icicles not only on houses. On **rock faces**, water seeps out of cracks in winter. It freezes and sometimes forms icicles several metres long and whole curtains of ice. Frozen **waterfalls** can form in this way too. In the mountains, skilled climbers even climb up such icefalls with ice axes and crampons. This is called **ice climbing**.

gewusst: Some icicles have small ridges all round that look like waves.
Similar-shaped formations of lime in caves are called stalactites, but they grow much more slowly.

teile.einleitung: Diamond is the hardest natural substance on Earth. It is made only of carbon and sparkles especially beautifully when it is cut. Diamonds are precious jewellery and useful tools at the same time.
wichtigste: Diamond is the hardest natural material.
It is made only of carbon.
Its weight is measured in carats; one carat is 0.2 grams.
A diamond with a special round cut is called a brilliant.
Diamonds are very hard, but also brittle.
They are used in drills and saws.

abschnitte.text: A **diamond** is made only of **carbon**. This is the same substance that coal is mostly made of. But in a diamond the carbon particles are joined to each other especially firmly and regularly. Diamonds form deep inside the Earth under very high **pressure** and great **heat**. Sometimes they reach the surface during volcanic eruptions.

Diamond is the **hardest natural material**. On the Mohs hardness scale it has the highest value, **10**. It can scratch almost all other substances, including **glass**. Even so, it is **brittle**. If you hit it hard with a hammer, it can shatter.

Most diamonds in jewellery are **colourless and clear**. But there are also rare coloured diamonds, for example yellow, blue or pink ones. A diamond with a special round cut is called a **brilliant**. The many small faces bounce the light back and forth inside the stone. That is why it sparkles so much.

The weight of diamonds and other gemstones is given in **carats**. **One carat is 0.2 grams**. The name probably comes from the seeds of the carob tree, which were once used as weights. Large diamonds are very rare and therefore especially valuable.

Because diamonds are so hard, they are used in **drills** and **saws**. With them you can even cut hard stone and concrete. For such tools, small diamonds that are not good enough for jewellery are usually used. Today **artificial diamonds** are also made in factories. They are also made of pure carbon.

gewusst: A pencil also contains carbon, as soft graphite. Diamond and graphite are made of the same substance.
At very high temperatures diamonds can burn in air, because they are made of carbon.

teile.einleitung: An ice age is a long period in the Earth's history when there are large ice sheets at the poles. The present ice age began about 2.6 million years ago. Since then cold and warm stages have taken turns, and right now we are living in a warm period.
wichtigste: The present ice age has been going on for about 2.6 million years.
Cold periods are called glacials, and the warm periods between them interglacials.
Today we live in the Holocene, a warm period.
In 1837 in Neuchâtel, Louis Agassiz made the idea of a great ice age well known.
At the peak of the last cold period, sea level was about 120 metres lower.
Erratic boulders in the Central Plateau were brought from the Alps by glaciers.

abschnitte.text: The present ice age began with the **Quaternary** about 2.6 million years ago. Since then **cold periods** and **warm periods** have taken turns many times. In scientific language, cold periods are called **glacials** and the warm periods between them **interglacials**. Today we live in the **Holocene**, a warm period. Because there are still large ice sheets at the poles, the ice age is nevertheless still going on.

abschnitte.titel: Glaciers as far as the Central Plateau
abschnitte.text: In the cold periods, the Alpine glaciers grew far out into the **Central Plateau**. They scooped out valleys and pushed rubble together into **moraines**. Many Swiss lakes lie in basins that the ice dug out. The glaciers also carried large boulders from the Alps. When the ice melted, these **erratic boulders** were left behind, often far from where they came from. Because so much water was locked up in the ice sheets, sea level was about **120 metres** lower than today.

The idea of an earlier great glaciation was developed to a large extent in Switzerland. As early as the 1820s, the Valais engineer **Ignaz Venetz** interpreted erratic boulders and moraines as traces of earlier, much larger glaciers. In 1837 the naturalist **Louis Agassiz** gave a famous speech in **Neuchâtel** about a great ice age. His ideas spread the ice age theory around the world.

In front of the glaciers lay a cold **steppe** with grasses and low plants. Large animals such as **mammoths** and **woolly rhinoceroses** lived there. With their thick coats they were well adapted to the cold. At **Niederweningen** in the canton of Zurich, several mammoth skeletons were found. Today you can visit a small mammoth museum there.

Even in a warm period the climate changes. From about 1350 to 1850 it was a little cooler than before and after. This period is called the **Little Ice Age**, although it was not a real cold period. Many Alpine glaciers reached their greatest length of the last few centuries around 1850. Since then they have been melting back strongly.

gewusst: Because sea level was so low, you could walk from England to France during the last cold period.
The Holocene has already lasted for about 11,700 years.

teile.einleitung: The Dufourspitze is the highest mountain in Switzerland. It lies in the canton of Valais near Zermatt, close to the border with Italy, and belongs to the mighty Monte Rosa massif. Its summit is covered with snow and ice all year round.
wichtigste: At 4634 metres above sea level, the Dufourspitze is the highest peak in Switzerland.
It is the highest peak of the Monte Rosa massif.
The peak used to be called the Gornerhorn.
In 1863 it was given its present name by decision of the Federal Council.
On 1 August 1855 people stood on the summit for the first time.
The famous Matterhorn stands very close by.

abschnitte.text: The Dufourspitze is **4634 metres** high. No other place in Switzerland is higher. The summit stands in the south of the canton of **Valais**, above Zermatt and very close to the border with Italy. At this height it is always cold. That is why there is **snow and ice** there all year round.

The Dufourspitze belongs to the **Monte Rosa massif**. A massif is a large group of mountains with several peaks. In the Monte Rosa massif there are several peaks over 4000 metres. Large glaciers flow down from the mountains, for example the **Gorner Glacier**. Not far away stands the **Matterhorn** with its pointed pyramid shape. It is world famous, but lower than the Dufourspitze.

The peak used to be called the **Gornerhorn**. In 1863 the Federal Council decided to name it after **Guillaume Henri Dufour**. Dufour was a general and an important mapmaker. Under his direction, the first accurate map of the whole of Switzerland was made, the **Dufour map**. So the name honours a man who had the Swiss mountains measured accurately for the first time.

On **1 August 1855** a roped party reached the summit for the first time. It was made up of British mountaineers and local **mountain guides**. This was a big event at a time when many Alpine peaks were being climbed for the first time. Today the ascent is still a demanding high-altitude climb over glaciers and rock. Many mountaineers spend the night before in the Monte Rosa Hut.

gewusst: The first ascent took place, of all days, on 1 August, which is now Switzerland's National Day.
After the Mont Blanc massif, the Monte Rosa massif is the second highest mountain massif in the Alps.

teile.einleitung: A rock crystal is a clear, see-through crystal that looks like glass or ice. It is a particularly pure form of quartz. In the Swiss Alps, crystal hunters have been searching for these glittering treasures for a long time.
wichtigste: A rock crystal is colourless and as clear as glass.
It is a six-sided column with a point at the top.
Rock crystal belongs to the quartz family of minerals.
In Switzerland, crystal hunters are called “Strahler”.
Rock crystals grow in hollows and cracks in the rock.
Large rock crystals need a very long time to grow.

abschnitte.text: A **rock crystal** is colourless and see-through. It is a very pure, clear form of **quartz**. Quartz is one of the most common minerals on Earth. But it is usually cloudy or coloured. Only when it is very pure does it become as clear as a rock crystal.

A rock crystal grows as a **column with six sides**. At the top it comes together in a **point**. This shape is no accident. The smallest building blocks of quartz always arrange themselves in the same pattern. That is why rock crystals from all over the world look similar.

Rock crystals grow in **cracks and hollows** in the rock. There, warm water with dissolved quartz flows through the rock. Over a long time, the quartz is deposited layer by layer. This happens very slowly, and large crystals need a very long time. In Switzerland, rock crystals are found mainly in the **Alps**; the areas around the **Grimsel** and the **Gotthard** are particularly well known.

In Switzerland, people who search for crystals in the mountains are called **“Strahler”**. They climb around the Alps looking for cracks in the rock where crystals might be hidden. The work is tiring and often dangerous. Some finds are so beautiful that they are now on display in museums.

In the past, many people believed that rock crystal was **ice that never melts**. After all, it feels cool and is as clear as ice. The word **crystal** comes from the Greek word for ice. Today we know that rock crystal is a mineral and has nothing to do with frozen water.

gewusst: The word crystal comes from the Greek word for ice.
Very large and famous rock crystals have been found in the area of the Grimsel and the Gotthard.

teile.einleitung: A barometer is an instrument that measures air pressure. Air pressure tells you a lot about the coming weather and about the height you are at. The barometer was invented in Italy in the 17th century.
wichtigste: In 1643 Evangelista Torricelli built the first mercury barometer.
At normal air pressure at sea level, the column of mercury is 760 millimetres high.
The aneroid barometer works without liquid, using an almost airless metal box.
If the barometer falls quickly, the weather usually gets worse.
Altimeters work on the principle of the barometer.
In 1648 Blaise Pascal showed that air pressure decreases with height.

abschnitte.text: In 1643 the Italian **Evangelista Torricelli**, a pupil of Galileo Galilei, filled a glass tube with **mercury**. Then he stood it upside down in a dish of mercury. The metal only sank a little way and then stayed where it was. This is because the air presses on the dish and holds the column in the tube in place. So for the first time air pressure became visible and measurable.

At normal air pressure at sea level, the column of mercury is **760 millimetres** high. That is where the old unit **millimetres of mercury** comes from. Mercury is very heavy, so a tube of less than a metre is enough. Water is about 13.6 times lighter than mercury. A water barometer would therefore need a column of just over **10 metres**.

In 1648 the French scholar **Blaise Pascal** had a barometer carried up the mountain **Puy de Dôme**. His brother-in-law carried it up. At the top, the mercury column was clearly lower than in the valley. This proved that air pressure decreases with height. The **altimeter**, which mountain walkers and pilots use, is based on this principle.

Many barometers at home are **aneroid barometers**. They contain a thin-walled, almost airless metal box. When air pressure is high, the box is squeezed together; when pressure is low, it expands. A pointer passes this small movement on to a scale. Such instruments are handy and do not need poisonous mercury.

If the barometer falls sharply within a few hours, a **low-pressure area** is usually approaching. Wind, clouds and rain often follow. If the air pressure rises, better weather is often on the way. What matters most is the change, not just a single value. Weather services such as MeteoSwiss measure air pressure at many stations.

gewusst: The word barometer comes from Greek and means roughly “weight measurer”.
The unit of air pressure, the pascal, is named after Blaise Pascal.

teile.einleitung: The Coriolis force deflects moving bodies on the rotating Earth. It decides how winds flow around high and low pressure areas. In physics it is an apparent force that only appears in a rotating frame of reference.
wichtigste: The Coriolis force is an inertial force, that is, an apparent force.
The Coriolis parameter is f = 2Ω·sin φ.
At the equator the horizontal Coriolis force is zero, at the poles it is greatest.
In the Northern Hemisphere it deflects to the right, in the Southern Hemisphere to the left.
In the geostrophic wind, the pressure gradient force and the Coriolis force balance each other.
It is named after Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis, who described it in 1835.

abschnitte.text: The **Coriolis force** only appears in a **rotating frame of reference** such as the Earth. Seen from outside, a body moves straight ahead while the Earth keeps turning beneath it. To an observer on the Earth, it looks as if the body is being deflected. That is why it is called an **inertial force** or **apparent force**. It was described in 1835 by the French physicist **Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis** in a paper about rotating machines.

The strength of the horizontal deflection is described by the **Coriolis parameter** f = 2Ω·sin φ. Here Ω is the angular velocity of the Earth, about 7.29 · 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹, and φ is the latitude. At the **equator**, sin 0° equals 0, so there is no horizontal deflection there. At the **poles**, f is greatest. At 45° latitude you get f = 2 · 7.29 · 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹ · 0.707, about **1.0 · 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹**. Switzerland lies close to 46° latitude, so the value is very similar.

In the **Northern Hemisphere**, moving air is deflected to the **right** of its direction of motion. In the **Southern Hemisphere** the sign of f is negative, and the deflection is to the **left**. That is why low-pressure areas turn anticlockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere. According to **Buys Ballot's law**, if you stand with your back to the wind in the Northern Hemisphere, the low lies to your **front left**. It is shifted forwards because of friction with the ground.

In the free atmosphere, high above the ground, there is hardly any friction. There the **pressure gradient force** and the **Coriolis force** balance each other. The wind that results is called the **geostrophic wind**. It does not blow straight from the high into the low, but **parallel to the isobars**, the lines of equal air pressure. That is why weather maps are easy to read: isobars that are close together mean strong wind.

The Earth's rotation can be made visible with a **Foucault pendulum**. The plane in which it swings seems to turn slowly, because the Earth is turning beneath it. At the **North Pole**, a full turn takes about one **sidereal day**, about 23 hours 56 minutes. At middle latitudes it takes longer, because the effect decreases with the sine of the latitude. At the equator the plane of swinging does not turn at all.

gewusst: The Coriolis force is far too weak to decide which way water spins down the plughole of a bath; other influences decide that.
Léon Foucault demonstrated his famous pendulum in Paris in 1851.

teile.einleitung: A doline is a funnel-shaped or bowl-shaped hollow in the ground. It forms in areas with easily dissolved rock such as limestone or gypsum. Such landscapes are called karst.
wichtigste: Dolines are hollows in karst areas.
A solution doline forms when rock is slowly dissolved from above.
A collapse doline forms when the roof of a hollow space caves in.
Dolines form in limestone, and especially quickly in gypsum.
Several dolines that have grown together make an uvala.
The word doline comes from Slovenian.

abschnitte.text: Rainwater takes up a little carbon dioxide from the air and the soil and so becomes slightly acidic. This means it can slowly dissolve **limestone**. **Gypsum** dissolves even more easily than limestone. That is why caves, cracks and hollows form in areas with such rock. These landscapes are called **karst**. Typical karst areas in Switzerland are in the **Jura** and in the **limestone Alps**.

In places where especially large amounts of water soak away, the rock is dissolved more strongly. The surface there sinks very gradually. This creates a bowl-shaped hollow, a **solution doline**. This process takes a very long time. Some areas are dotted with hundreds of such hollows.

Sometimes water dissolves a **hollow space** beneath the surface. If the roof above it becomes too thin, it caves in. A steep funnel forms, a **collapse doline**. This can happen suddenly. That is why dolines can be dangerous for **houses and roads**, because buildings or roadways can sink.

At the bottom of a doline there is often a **swallow hole**, also called a **ponor**. There a stream suddenly disappears into the ground and flows on underground. If several neighbouring dolines grow together, a larger, irregular hollow forms. It is called an **uvala**.

The word **“doline”** comes from **Slovenian**. There “dolina” means valley or hollow. Many technical words for karst come from the **Karst plateau** in Slovenia. These landforms were studied there early on. The word karst itself also goes back to this region.

gewusst: In karst areas there are often hardly any streams on the surface, because the water disappears underground.
The word uvala also comes from a South Slavic language.

teile.einleitung: In a thunderstorm, a bright flash of lightning is followed by a loud bang or a long rumble: thunder. It is the sound that lightning makes in the air. If you watch lightning and thunder, you can even work out how far away a thunderstorm is.
wichtigste: Thunder is made because lightning suddenly heats the air very strongly.
The hot air expands explosively, and we hear this as a bang.
Sound takes about 3 seconds to travel one kilometre.
The seconds between lightning and thunder divided by three give the distance in kilometres.
If lightning and thunder come almost at the same time, the thunderstorm is very close.
After the last thunder, stay under shelter for about another 30 minutes.

abschnitte.text: A flash of lightning is a huge electrical discharge. In a fraction of a second it heats the air in a narrow channel to many thousands of degrees, according to estimates up to about **30,000 degrees**. The air suddenly expands. This creates a **pressure wave** that travels as sound. We hear this sound as thunder.

Light is so fast that we see the lightning practically at once. **Sound** is much slower and takes about 3 seconds to travel one kilometre. If you count, for example, 9 seconds between lightning and thunder, the thunderstorm is about 3 kilometres away. If the crash comes almost at the same time, the lightning is striking only a few hundred metres away. Then it is high time to stay indoors.

A flash of lightning is often several kilometres long. The sound from the nearby parts of the flash arrives first, and the sound from the more distant parts later. That is why we often hear not a short bang but a long **rumble** or roll. Mountains and hills also throw the sound back, like an echo. That is why thunder can echo for an especially long time in the mountains.

If you can hear thunder, you are close enough to be struck by lightning. You are safest in a building or a car. Lightning can still strike even at the end of a thunderstorm. That is why you wait about **half an hour** after the last thunder before going outside again. In Switzerland, thunderstorms happen mainly in summer, but rarely also in winter, sometimes even while it is snowing.

In the past people could not explain thunder. The Germanic peoples believed in the thunder god **Donar**. The German word for Thursday, **“Donnerstag”**, is named after him. In the Norse legends from Scandinavia, the thunder god is called **Thor**. When he hurled his hammer, so people said, it thundered in the sky.

gewusst: The English word “Thursday” means Thor's day.
Thunderstorms in winter with snowfall are sometimes called thundersnow.

teile.einleitung: Diagenesis is the name for all the changes that a loose sediment goes through after it has been deposited, until it has become solid rock. In this way sand becomes sandstone and mud becomes mudstone. Diagenesis ends where metamorphism begins.
wichtigste: Diagenesis is the hardening of loose sediment into sedimentary rock.
In compaction, sediment is squeezed together and loses pore water.
In cementation, minerals that come out of solution glue the grains together.
Angular rubble turns into breccia, rounded pebbles into conglomerate.
The change from peat to lignite to hard coal is called coalification.
At about 150 to 200 °C, diagenesis turns into metamorphism.

abschnitte.text: Rivers, wind and sea constantly deposit **sediments**: sand, gravel, mud or lime mud. Over time more and more layers settle on top. Under a growing **load** and at moderate temperatures, the loose sediments become solid **sedimentary rock**. All these changes after deposition are called **diagenesis**. It goes up to the boundary of **metamorphism**.

In **compaction**, the weight of the layers above squeezes the sediment together. The grains move closer together, and **pore water** is squeezed out. Clays in particular lose a large part of their pore space. In **cementation**, minerals such as **calcite**, **quartz** or **iron oxides** come out of the pore water. They glue the grains together into solid rock like putty.

Coarse fragments turn into coarse-grained rocks through diagenesis. If the pieces are **angular**, they were hardly transported. The hardened rock is then called **breccia**. **Rounded pebbles** turn into a **conglomerate**. A well-known conglomerate in Switzerland is **Nagelfluh**, from which the Rigi and the Napf, for example, are built.

Plant remains also change during diagenesis. As they are buried deeper, **peat** turns into **lignite** and later into **hard coal**. This process is called **coalification**. With pressure and temperature the carbon content rises, while water and volatile substances escape. At the end of the series is the very carbon-rich **anthracite**.

When solutions rich in magnesium flow through limestone, magnesium replaces part of the calcium. This produces the mineral **dolomite**, CaMg(CO₃)₂; the process is called **dolomitisation**. Dolomite builds large parts of the **Dolomites** in Italy. Under high pressure, calcite is dissolved where grains touch. Insoluble remains such as clay are left behind as dark zigzag lines, the **stylolites**. From about **150 to 200 °C**, typical metamorphic minerals form, and diagenesis then turns into metamorphism.

gewusst: Stylolites look like jagged seams and can often be seen well on polished slabs of limestone.
The Dolomites are named after the mineral dolomite, and the mineral after the French scientist Déodat de Dolomieu.

teile.einleitung: Surf forms when waves break on the coast. The water foams white and sprays up high. Surf is beautiful to look at, but it can also be dangerous.
wichtigste: Surf is waves breaking on the coast.
Waves break because the water gets shallower towards the shore.
The foam is white because it contains many air bubbles.
The fine drops that spray up are called spray.
A rip current can pull swimmers out to sea.
If you get caught in a current, swim sideways, parallel to the beach.

abschnitte.text: Out at sea, the waves roll along evenly. As they approach the shore, the water gets **shallower**. At the bottom, the wave is slowed down by the sea floor. At the top it is faster, gets steeper, tips forwards and **breaks**. This breaking of waves on the coast is called **surf**.

When a wave breaks, a lot of **air** is mixed into the water. The many small bubbles make the foam look **white**. When waves crash against rocks, fine drops of water spray high into the air. These drops are called **spray**. On windy days you can see it flying far across the coast.

The water of the surf has to get back into the sea. It often flows quickly away from the beach in **narrow channels**. This **rip current** can pull swimmers out. The important thing is: stay calm and do not swim straight against the current towards the shore. It is better to swim **sideways, parallel to the beach**. The current is usually only narrow, so you get out of it and can then return to the shore.

The surf is always at work on the coast. The waves roll **stones** back and forth again and again. This grinds off the edges, and the stones become **round**. On cliffs, the surf gnaws at the rock and can carve out caves and rock arches. In a **storm**, the waves are especially high and the surf roars especially wildly.

gewusst: The round pebbles on many beaches were ground smooth by the surf over a long time.
Even on large Swiss lakes such as Lake Constance or Lake Geneva, there can be strong surf in a storm.

teile.einleitung: On 11 September 1881, a huge mass of rock crashed down into the valley near Elm in the canton of Glarus. The landslide cost 114 people their lives. One reason for the disaster was the quarrying of slate on the mountain.
wichtigste: Elm lies at the far end of the Sernf Valley in the canton of Glarus.
The landslide happened on 11 September 1881.
About 10 million cubic metres of rock broke away from the Plattenbergkopf.
114 people died and 83 buildings were destroyed.
Slate quarrying had undermined the slope.
The geologist Albert Heim studied the landslide closely.

abschnitte.text: **Elm** lies at the far end of the **Sernf Valley** in the canton of **Glarus**. Today it belongs to the municipality of **Glarus Süd**. In the 19th century the village was known for its **slate**. This rock can be split into thin slabs. Among other things, it was used to make writing slates and slate pencils for schoolchildren.

For years slate was quarried on the slope of the **Plattenbergkopf**. As a result, the mountain was more and more **undermined**. Cracks were already appearing in the rock before the disaster. In September 1881 it rained heavily. Together with the quarrying, this finally made the slope lose its hold.

On 11 September 1881, **two smaller falls** came down first. They attracted curious onlookers. Shortly afterwards came the **main fall**, which hit many of these people. About **10 million cubic metres** of rock crashed several hundred metres down. Then the mass spread out like a stream and flowed about **two kilometres** across the flat valley floor.
**114 people** died in the landslide. In addition, **83 buildings** were destroyed. It was one of the worst landslides in the history of Switzerland. Whole families lost relatives and their homes.

The Swiss geologist **Albert Heim** studied the landslide closely. Together with the pastor **Ernst Buss**, he published a report about it in the same year. His studies had a strong influence on **landslide research**.

gewusst: After falling, the mass of rock at Elm flowed about two kilometres further over flat ground.
Writing slates made of Glarus slate used to be used in many schools.

teile.einleitung: Copernicus is the Earth observation programme of the European Union. Satellites watch the land, sea and atmosphere and provide data for the environment, the climate and disaster protection. The data are free of charge for everyone.
wichtigste: Copernicus is run by the EU; ESA is responsible for the Sentinel satellites.
Before 2012 the programme was called GMES.
Sentinel-1 carries a C-band radar.
Sentinel-2 provides pictures with a resolution of up to 10 metres.
Sentinel-5P measures trace gases such as nitrogen dioxide with TROPOMI.
Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich measures sea level.
The data are freely available to everyone.

abschnitte.text: **Copernicus** is funded and run by the **European Union**. The European Space Agency **ESA** is responsible for the **Sentinel satellites**. Some of them are operated by the weather satellite organisation **EUMETSAT**. The programme used to be called **GMES**, short for Global Monitoring for Environment and Security. In 2012 it was given the name of the astronomer **Nicolaus Copernicus**.

**Sentinel-1** carries a **C-band radar**. Radar sees through clouds and also works at night. The pictures are used, for example, to watch sea ice, floods and **ground movements** with the method called InSAR. **Sentinel-2** measures in 13 spectral channels, the finest with **10 metres** per pixel. Together, two such satellites take a picture of the same place on the equator every **5 days**, and even more often at higher latitudes.

**Sentinel-5P** carries the spectrometer **TROPOMI**. It covers the whole Earth every day and measures **trace gases** such as nitrogen dioxide, ozone, methane and carbon monoxide. **Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich** uses **radar altimetry** to measure the height of the sea surface to within a few centimetres. It continues a series of measurements of global **sea level** that has been running since 1992.

The **Copernicus Emergency Management Service** helps after disasters. After floods, fires or earthquakes, satellite pictures are turned into **damage maps** within hours. These maps help rescue teams with their planning. In this way they can quickly see which roads, bridges or villages are affected.

An **open data policy** applies to the Sentinel data. They are available to everyone **freely and free of charge**. Anyone can download them from online portals. This has led to them being used a lot in research, by authorities and in business. In Switzerland, too, experts use Sentinel pictures to keep track of glaciers, forests or fields, for example.

gewusst: Sentinel-6 is named after the American scientist Michael Freilich, who led NASA's Earth observation.
Radar satellites such as Sentinel-1 can detect ground movements of a few millimetres.

teile.einleitung: In an upwelling zone, cold water rises from the depths of the ocean to the surface. This water brings many nutrients with it. That is why upwelling zones are among the most fertile regions of the seas.
wichtigste: In upwelling, cold deep water replaces surface water that has been carried away.
The deep water is rich in nutrients such as nitrate and phosphate.
The large coastal upwelling zones lie on the west coasts of the continents at low latitudes.
Ekman transport pushes the surface water away from the coast.
There is also upwelling at the equator in the Pacific.
A large part of the world's fish catch comes from upwelling zones.
Deserts such as the Atacama or the Namib often lie on such coasts.

abschnitte.text: The water at the sea surface is usually warmer than the water deep down. When the surface water is pushed away, cold water flows in from below. This process is called **upwelling**. The deep water contains many nutrients such as **nitrate** and **phosphate**, because dead organisms are broken down there. In the upwelling zone, these nutrients reach the sunlight.

On the west coasts of the continents, winds often blow along the coast towards the equator. Because the Earth turns, the moving surface water is deflected sideways. This shift is called **Ekman transport**, named after a Swedish ocean scientist. It carries the water out to the open sea, and cold water wells up from below at the coast. Well-known examples are off **Peru and Chile**, Namibia, California and north-west Africa.

There is also upwelling in the middle of the Pacific at the equator. There the **trade winds** blow westwards on both sides of the equator. Ekman transport deflects the water to the north north of the equator and to the south south of it. So the water moves apart, which experts call **divergence**. Cold deep water rises into the gap that forms.

The many nutrients make a great deal of **plankton** grow. Plankton is food for small fish, which in turn are food for larger animals. Upwelling zones cover only a small part of the sea's surface, but they provide a large part of the world's fish catch. In the Humboldt Current off Peru, the **Peruvian anchovy**, also called anchoveta, lives in huge shoals. It is mainly made into fishmeal and fish oil.

The cold upwelling water cools the air directly above it. Cold air below and warmer air above form a stable layering, a so-called **inversion**. Moist air can then hardly rise, and no rain clouds form. That is why deserts such as the **Atacama** in Chile and the **Namib** in Namibia lie on such coasts. Instead, thick **coastal fog** often forms when moist sea air cools down over the cold water.

gewusst: In Chile the coastal fog is called camanchaca. There people catch water droplets from the fog with large fog nets.
Although the Atacama lies right by the sea, it is one of the driest places on Earth.

teile.einleitung: The carbon footprint shows how many greenhouse gases a person, a product or a company causes. It helps us to understand which activities put a heavy burden on the climate. These include heating, travelling, eating and shopping.
wichtigste: The carbon footprint adds up all the greenhouse gases caused.
It is usually given in tonnes of CO2 equivalents per year.
Other gases such as methane or nitrous oxide are converted into their CO2 effect.
The bicycle has a very small footprint per passenger kilometre.
Beef usually has the largest footprint per kilogram of any food.
Embodied energy is the energy used to make, transport and dispose of products.
The oil company BP made the personal footprint well known from 2004.

abschnitte.text: The **carbon footprint** adds up all the **greenhouse gases** that someone or something causes. Greenhouse gases hold heat in the atmosphere and so warm the climate. The footprint includes, for example, **heating**, **transport**, **food** and **consumption**. You can calculate it for a person, a family, a product or a company. For a person it is usually given in **tonnes per year**.

As well as carbon dioxide, there are other greenhouse gases such as **methane** or **nitrous oxide**. For the same amount, they cause more warming than CO2. So that everything can be added up, their amount is converted into the equivalent amount of CO2. The result is called **CO2 equivalents**. In this way very different activities can be compared with each other.

Means of transport cause very different amounts of greenhouse gases. When you **cycle**, no fuel is burned. Only making the bike and a little extra food count. That is why the footprint per passenger kilometre is very small. Trains and buses also usually do better than cars, while air travel has a large footprint.

There are big differences in food too. **Cattle** need a lot of feed and land and give off methane. That is why a kilogram of **beef** causes many times the emissions of plant foods. The **season** also matters. In winter, no strawberries grow outdoors in Switzerland. They then often come by aeroplane or from heated greenhouses, which uses a lot of energy.

Every product contains **embodied energy**. This is the energy needed to make, transport and dispose of it, for example with a mobile phone or a house. It often makes up a large part of the footprint. The personal footprint became well known from **2004** through an advertising campaign with a calculator by the oil company **BP**. Critics say that this shifted responsibility from companies onto individual people. Others still find the calculator useful for understanding their own behaviour.

gewusst: A mobile phone causes a large part of its footprint while it is being made, before you even switch it on.
Methane from the stomachs of cattle is an important greenhouse gas.

teile.einleitung: An iceberg is a huge block of ice floating in the sea. It has broken off a glacier. The dangerous thing about it: most of it lies hidden under water.
wichtigste: Only about a tenth of an iceberg can be seen above the water.
Icebergs are made of fresh water, not of frozen seawater.
When a piece of ice breaks off a glacier into the sea, this is called calving.
Most large icebergs come from Greenland and Antarctica.
In warmer water an iceberg slowly melts.
Very old, dense ice can glow blue.

abschnitte.text: In **Greenland** and **Antarctica**, huge glaciers flow all the way into the sea. At the edge, large pieces of ice keep breaking off and crashing into the water. This process is called **calving**. This is how a new iceberg forms. In Antarctica, flat, very large icebergs sometimes break off; these are **tabular icebergs**.

abschnitte.titel: Only the tip can be seen
abschnitte.text: Ice is a little lighter than water, which is why it floats. But it is only a little lighter. That is why most of an iceberg is **under water**, and only about a tenth sticks out. This is where the saying “only the tip of the iceberg” comes from. It means that only a small part of a problem can be seen.

abschnitte.titel: Fresh ice in the salty sea
abschnitte.text: Although icebergs float in the salty sea, they are made of **fresh water**. Their ice formed from **snow** that built up on the glacier over many years. Very dense, old ice contains hardly any air bubbles. It swallows red light and therefore looks **blue**. When an iceberg drifts into warmer water, it melts bit by bit until nothing is left.

Because you cannot see most of an iceberg, icebergs are dangerous for ships. In 1912 the **Titanic** hit an iceberg in the North Atlantic and sank. After that an international **ice patrol** was set up, which watches icebergs and warns ships. Today satellites and radar also help with this.

gewusst: Some icebergs from Antarctica are bigger than a whole Swiss canton.
When glacier ice melts it crackles, because old air bubbles under pressure burst.

teile.einleitung: If you dig a deep hole in the ground, you can see layers of different colours. In scientific language these layers of soil are called horizons. Each layer is different and has its own job.
wichtigste: The layers of the soil are called horizons.
At the very top lies the dark topsoil, rich in humus.
Below it comes the lighter subsoil.
At the very bottom lies the solid parent rock.
Most earthworms live in the upper layers.
On building sites the topsoil is removed and stored.

abschnitte.text: You can see the layers of soil best if you dig a **deep hole**. In the wall of the pit you can make out stripes of different colours from top to bottom. Experts call these layers **horizons**. All the horizons together make up the **soil profile**. Every soil has a slightly different profile, depending on the rock, the climate and the plants.

At the very top lies the **topsoil**. Leaves and plant remains fall here. Small animals, fungi and bacteria break them down into **humus**. That is why this layer is usually the darkest and most fertile. Most **earthworms** also live here, because they eat plant remains and humus.

Below the topsoil lies the **subsoil**. It is **lighter** because it contains less humus. On the other hand, substances that rainwater has washed out from above often collect here. The roots of large plants reach down into the subsoil. There they find water and nutrients.

At the very bottom lies **solid rock**. The soil once formed from it, which is why it is called the **parent rock**. Over a very long time, the rock breaks down because of water, frost and plant roots. Slowly, new soil forms from it. One centimetre of soil often takes many decades or even longer to form.

The humus-rich topsoil is very valuable. That is why on **building sites** it is often removed first and stored. Later it can be used again for gardens and fields. In Switzerland there are rules so that this soil is not simply thrown away.

gewusst: A single spoonful of good garden soil contains more living things than there are people on Earth.
In scientific language, soil layers have letters; the topsoil, for example, is called the A horizon.

teile.einleitung: A thin section is a wafer-thin slice of rock that is glued onto a glass slide. When ground so thin, most minerals let light through. Under the microscope you can then see what a rock is made of.
wichtigste: A standard rock thin section is about 30 micrometres thick, that is, 0.03 millimetres.
Only when they are this thin do most minerals become see-through.
In the past the slices were glued on with Canada balsam, today mostly with epoxy resin.
Between crossed polarisers, minerals show typical interference colours.
From about 1850 Henry Clifton Sorby made thin sections usable for the study of rocks.
Archaeology also uses thin sections, for example of pottery fragments.

abschnitte.titel: How a thin section is made
abschnitte.text: First a small slab is sawn from the rock. One side is ground smooth and glued onto a glass **microscope slide**. Then the slab is ground thinner and thinner until it is only about **30 micrometres** thick. Traditionally **Canada balsam**, a clear resin from the balsam fir, was used as the glue. Today **epoxy resin** is mostly used.

The thin section is studied with a **polarising microscope**. It only lets through light that vibrates in one particular direction. When two such filters are crossed, many minerals show glowing **interference colours**. These colours depend on the **double refraction** of the mineral and on the thickness of the section. That is why the same standard thickness is so important. Quartz, for example, appears grey to white at standard thickness.

Some minerals, especially **ore minerals**, stay black even in a thin section. They are called **opaque**. They are studied in **reflected light** on polished sections. Researchers look at how strongly and in what colour they reflect light. To work out the shares of the minerals, there is the **point counting method**: at many points on a grid, you count which mineral is under the crosshairs.

From about 1850 the British natural scientist **Henry Clifton Sorby** from Sheffield was the first to study rocks systematically under the microscope. He is regarded as the founder of microscopic **petrography**, the study of rocks. Today geologists use thin sections all over the world. **Archaeology** also uses them: the grains in the clay of pottery fragments reveal where the raw material came from.

gewusst: A thin section is thinner than a human hair.
Sorby also studied steel under the microscope and is therefore also seen as a pioneer of metallography.

teile.einleitung: A mountain lake lies high up in the mountains. It is often small, cold and very clear. There are hundreds of such lakes in Switzerland, and many of them formed in the Ice Age.
wichtigste: A mountain lake is a lake high up in the mountains.
Many mountain lakes are filled with meltwater from snow and glaciers.
During the Ice Age, glaciers scooped out many hollows.
Fine rock flour colours some mountain lakes turquoise.
When there is no wind, the mountains are reflected in the still water.
The Oeschinensee lies above Kandersteg in the Bernese Oberland.

abschnitte.text: Many mountain lakes formed during the **Ice Age**. At that time huge **glaciers** covered the Alps. The heavy ice ground deep hollows into the rock. When the glaciers melted, these hollows filled with water. Other mountain lakes formed because a rockslide or glacier rubble blocked a valley.

The water in mountain lakes is usually very cold. It often comes from **snow and glaciers**. Also, it is cool high up, and many mountain lakes are frozen over for months. Because little dirt gets in, the water is often very clear. When there is no wind, the surface is as smooth as a **mirror**, and you can see the mountains in it.

Some mountain lakes glow **turquoise**. The reason is fine **rock flour**. Glaciers grind the rock beneath them into very fine dust. This floats in the water and scatters the sunlight. That makes the lake look a glowing colour.

One of the best-known mountain lakes in Switzerland is the **Oeschinensee** above **Kandersteg** in the Bernese Oberland. It is surrounded by high rock walls. In summer many people hike there, and in winter it freezes over.

Only animals that can cope with the cold live in the cold water. One of them is the **trout**. It likes cold water that is **rich in oxygen**. This is because cold water can hold more oxygen than warm water. That is why trout like living in mountain lakes and mountain streams.

gewusst: Some mountain lakes are covered with ice for more than half the year.
The turquoise colour of many glacier lakes comes from tiny grains of rock in the water.

teile.einleitung: Calcite is one of the most common minerals on Earth. It is made of calcium carbonate and builds up limestone, marble and stalactites and stalagmites. Clear calcite crystals play an amazing trick with light.
wichtigste: Calcite is made of calcium carbonate with the formula CaCO3.
It is also called calc-spar.
On the Mohs scale it has a hardness of 3.
Calcite fizzes with dilute hydrochloric acid.
Clear calcite shows double refraction: writing appears twice.
Limestone, marble and dripstones are made mainly of calcite.
Aragonite has the same formula but a different crystal structure.

abschnitte.text: **Calcite** is made of **calcium carbonate** with the formula **CaCO3**. Another name for it is **calc-spar**. On the **Mohs scale**, calcite is the reference mineral for hardness 3. You can only just scratch it with a copper coin, and easily with a knife. Calcite is often white or colourless, but it can also be yellow, pink or other colours.

If you put a drop of **dilute hydrochloric acid** on calcite, it foams and fizzes. The acid breaks down the calcium carbonate. In doing so, **carbon dioxide** escapes in small bubbles. With this simple test, geologists can recognise limestone rocks even out in the field.

If you look at writing through a clear calcite crystal, you see it **twice**. The crystal splits every ray of light into two rays. This is called **double refraction**. It is especially clear in **Iceland spar**. When calcite is split, it breaks into **slanted cubes**, so-called **rhombohedra**, because it splits in three directions that are not at right angles.

**Limestone** often forms from the shells and skeletons of sea creatures. **Marble** forms when limestone is changed by pressure and heat. Both are made mainly of calcite. Large parts of the Jura and of the limestone Alps of Switzerland are built of limestone. That is why calcite plays a big part in the Swiss landscape.

Rainwater dissolves lime in the rock. When it drips down in a cave, the dissolved mineral is deposited again. This is how **stalactites and stalagmites** grow, for example in the **Hölloch** cave in the Muotathal. The mineral **aragonite** has the same formula as calcite but a different crystal structure. Mussels build their shimmering **mother-of-pearl** from tiny plates of aragonite.

gewusst: Limescale in a kettle is also mostly calcium carbonate.
Centuries ago, researchers were already studying double refraction in Iceland spar.

teile.einleitung: A floodplain is an area beside a river that is flooded again and again. Floodplains are among the habitats with the most species in Switzerland, and at the same time they protect against floods.
wichtigste: Floodplains lie along rivers and are regularly flooded during high water.
Willows and poplars are typical of the softwood floodplain forest.
Floodplains hold back floodwater and slow down the flood wave.
Floods keep creating new habitats for many species.
Since 1992 the most important floodplains have been listed in a federal inventory.
Well-known floodplains are the Bolle di Magadino and the Pfynwald.

abschnitte.text: **Floodplains** lie along rivers and streams. During **floods** they are regularly covered with water and then dry out again. The river deposits gravel and sand, tears away trees and digs new channels. So a floodplain is always changing. This **dynamism** is what makes it special.

Right next to the water grows the **softwood floodplain forest**. **Willows** and **poplars** are typical. They can bear long floods and grow quickly. A little further away from the river, where water reaches less often, comes the **hardwood floodplain forest** with trees such as ash and oak.

Floods keep creating new and varied habitats: **gravel banks**, **ponds**, wet and dry places, young and old woods. In this **patchwork** a particularly large number of animal and plant species live. The **beaver** also helps to shape floodplains. It had died out in Switzerland and was reintroduced from **1956**. With its dams it holds back streams and creates new wetlands.

In a floodplain, a river can **spread out** during a flood. The water is held back, and downstream the water levels rise less. Many rivers in Switzerland were straightened and dammed in the past. Today some are being **restored** so that they get more space.

Since **1992** the most valuable floodplains have been listed in the **Federal Inventory of Alluvial Zones of National Importance**. The cantons have to preserve them and, where possible, improve them.
