In Ticino, the **Bolle di Magadino** lie where the River Ticino flows into Lake Maggiore, a resting place for many migratory birds. In Valais, the Rhône is still allowed to split into branches in the **Pfynwald**, in the **Pfyn-Finges** nature park.

gewusst: A large part of Switzerland's former floodplains has disappeared because of river engineering.
The Bolle di Magadino are also protected internationally as a wetland.

teile.einleitung: On 2 September 1806, an enormous mass of rock broke away from the Rossberg in the canton of Schwyz. It buried the village of Goldau and other hamlets. The Goldau landslide is one of the greatest natural disasters in Swiss history.
wichtigste: The landslide happened on 2 September 1806.
The mass of rock broke away from the southern flank of the Rossberg.
457 people died in the disaster.
Almost 40 million cubic metres of rock crashed into the valley.
Softened layers of marl acted as a slide for the conglomerate rock.
Part of the mass rushed into Lake Lauerz and set off a flood wave.
Today the Goldau Nature and Animal Park lies in the field of rubble.

abschnitte.titel: Between the Rossberg and the Rigi
abschnitte.text: **Goldau** belongs to the municipality of **Arth** in the canton of **Schwyz**. The village lies between **Lake Zug** and **Lake Lauerz**. On one side of the valley rises the **Rossberg**, on the other the **Rigi**. On 2 September 1806 a huge mass of rock broke away from the southern flank of the Rossberg, below the Gnipenspitze. It raced into the valley and on the other side even surged up the Rigi.

The Rossberg is made of tilted layers of **Nagelfluh**, a conglomerate. This is a rock made of cemented pebbles that is widespread in the foothills of the Alps. Between these layers lie thin layers of **marl**. After a lot of rain, water got in through cracks and softened the marl. The blocks of rock then slid off it as if on a **slide**.

Experts estimate the mass at almost **40 million cubic metres**. It buried an area of about 6.5 square kilometres. As a rule, a **landslide** of this kind is defined as at least about one million cubic metres. Smaller falls are called **rockfalls**. So Goldau was far bigger than the threshold for a landslide.

**457 people** died in the landslide, and over 300 animals were killed too. Several villages and hamlets were buried. Part of the mass rushed into **Lake Lauerz**. As a result, the lake became about one seventh smaller. Eyewitnesses reported a **flood wave about 20 metres high**.

The large boulders still shape the landscape today. Right in the middle of the field of rubble lies the **Goldau Nature and Animal Park**. Native animals live there between the boulders. A museum recalls the disaster of 1806. You can still see the traces of the place where the rock broke away on the Rossberg.

gewusst: The mass of rock was so enormous that it surged up the Rigi on the other side of the valley.
The landslide made Lake Lauerz about one seventh smaller.

teile.einleitung: A stream is a small flowing body of water. It is narrower than a river and often babbles through woods, meadows and mountains. Many animals and plants live in and beside a stream.
wichtigste: A stream is a small, flowing body of water.
Because of gravity, water always flows downhill.
The steeper the land, the faster the stream flows.
When many streams flow together, a river forms.
Brown trout and freshwater shrimps need clean, cool water.
The dipper dives into the stream for small animals.

abschnitte.text: A stream often begins at a **spring**, where water comes out of the ground, or it collects rain and meltwater. Because water always flows downwards due to **gravity**, a stream always runs downhill. On the way, more streams join it. So the body of water keeps getting bigger until it becomes a **river**. In Switzerland there are countless streams that finally flow into rivers such as the Rhine, the Rhône or the Aare.

In the mountains the land is often very steep. That is why a **mountain stream** rushes quickly and powerfully over stones. In flat country, on the other hand, a stream flows calmly and often bends. The fast water carries sand and small stones with it. Where it slows down, they are left behind again.

The **brown trout** needs cool water with plenty of oxygen and lives in many Swiss streams. The **freshwater shrimp** hides under the stones. If you find a lot of them, the water is clean. The **dipper** is a small songbird that even walks along the bed of the stream under water, looking for small animals. The **beaver** also lives by streams. It dams them with branches and mud to make a pond, in which it can build its lodge safely.

The ground on a stream bank is often wet. Plants that like a lot of water grow there. In spring the yellow flowers of the **marsh marigold** shine brightly. Trees such as alders and willows hold the bank in place with their roots and give shade. The shade keeps the water cool, which the fish like.

gewusst: Freshwater shrimps help experts to tell how clean a stream is.
The dipper can dive and walk along the bottom of the stream under water.

teile.einleitung: The Alps consist of a stack of huge slabs of rock that have been pushed on top of each other over many kilometres. Geologists call such slabs nappes. The theory of nappes was developed to a large extent from the Swiss Alps.
wichtigste: A nappe is a mass of rock that has been pushed a long way over other rocks.
Autochthonous rocks still lie where they formed, while allochthonous ones were transported.
A klippe is an isolated remnant of a nappe left by erosion, such as the Mythen.
In 1893 Hans Schardt interpreted the Préalpes romandes as nappes.
In 1902 Maurice Lugeon applied the theory of nappes to the whole of the Alps.
In eastern Switzerland, from bottom to top, lie the Helvetic, the Penninic and the Austroalpine.
The Morcles nappe is a prime example of a fold nappe.

abschnitte.text: A **nappe** is a large slab of rock that has been **sheared off** from what lay beneath it and pushed over other rocks for many kilometres. This happened as the Alps formed, when Africa and Europe were moving towards each other. Rocks that still lie where they formed are called **autochthonous**, which means “formed on the spot”. Nappes that have been carried a long way are called **allochthonous**. The area a nappe comes from is called its **root zone**. Many nappes of the Swiss Alps have their roots far to the south.

The very front end of a nappe in the direction of movement is called the **nappe front**. As it moves forward, it is often rolled downwards into a lying fold. Some nappes are huge lying folds with an overturned lower limb. Such **fold nappes** are shown particularly beautifully by the **Morcles nappe** in Lower Valais. It can be seen well at the **Rhône bend** between Saint-Maurice and Martigny.

When **erosion** has removed a nappe all around, sometimes only a single remnant is left. Such a remnant is called a **klippe**. A well-known example is the **Mythen** near Schwyz. They are made of foreign rock that was pushed here from far to the south. That is why this older rock now lies on top of younger rocks.

For a long time people did not understand how the Alps were built. In **1893** **Hans Schardt** recognised that the rocks of the **Préalpes romandes** do not match what lies beneath them and come from far away. With this he laid one of the foundations of the theory of nappes. In a great overview in **1902**, the Lausanne geologist **Maurice Lugeon** showed that the whole of the Alps can be explained by nappes pushed on top of each other. His work made the theory of nappes accepted around the world.

In eastern Switzerland the large nappe systems lie like this, from bottom to top: **Helvetic**, **Penninic** and **Austroalpine**. The stack reflects the original order from north to south. What was deposited furthest north lies at the bottom. What came from the south was pushed over it. In the area of the **Swiss Tectonic Arena Sardona** in the Glarus region, such a thrust can be seen particularly well; it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

gewusst: On the summits of the Mythen, older rock lies on top of younger rock, because it was pushed here from far to the south.
At the Glarus thrust, older rocks lie sharply separated on top of much younger ones.

teile.einleitung: Ice is frozen water. When water cools below 0 °C, it becomes solid and forms crystals. In everyday life we meet ice as ice cubes, icicles or black ice, and in nature as glaciers or as huge icebergs in the sea.
wichtigste: Ice is water in solid form; it forms below 0 °C.
Ice floats in water because it is lighter than liquid water.
Pointed rods of ice hanging from a roof are called icicles.
A huge chunk of ice floating in the sea is called an iceberg.
It is dangerous on a frozen lake, because the ice can break.
In winter salt is spread on the roads so that the ice melts.
Glaciers are huge masses of ice that move slowly.

abschnitte.text: Ice is **frozen water**. When water cools to 0 °C, the water particles arrange themselves into a regular pattern. This creates **ice crystals**, which are often six-sided, as you can see in snowflakes. When it gets warmer than 0 °C, the ice melts back into water. The point at which water freezes is called the **freezing point**.

Most substances become denser when they turn solid. Water is an exception: ice is about 9 per cent lighter than liquid water, because its crystal pattern has many gaps. That is why ice **floats** on top. So lakes freeze from the top down, and underneath the water stays liquid, so fish can survive. This special property is called the **anomaly of water**.

In nature ice comes in many forms. **Glaciers** form when snow builds up over many years and is pressed together into ice. The largest glacier in the Alps is the Great Aletsch Glacier in Valais. When ice breaks off glaciers into the sea, an **iceberg** forms, of which only about a tenth sticks out of the water. In winter **icicles** grow on gutters when meltwater drips down and freezes again.

On a frozen lake the **ice can break**, especially when it is still thin or lies over places where streams flow in. You should only go onto ice that has been declared safe by the municipality. On roads and pavements, **black ice** sometimes forms, on which you can easily slip. Falling icicles can injure people. If someone falls through, do not go onto the ice yourself, but get help and call the number 112.

In winter, municipalities spread **salt** on the roads. Salt water only freezes at lower temperatures than pure water. That is why ice melts when salt lies on it, as long as it is not too cold. But because salt harms plants and soils, some municipalities prefer to use **grit** made of small stones on pavements. It does not melt the ice, but it makes it less slippery.

abschnitte.titel: Ice in everyday life and sport
abschnitte.text: Ice cubes cool drinks, and food stays fresh for a long time in the freezer. In the past people sawed ice out of lakes in winter and stored it in ice cellars to keep things cool in summer. In Switzerland **ice hockey** is one of the most popular sports. People skate on ice rinks and frozen mountain lakes such as Lake St Moritz. On Lake St Moritz there are even horse races in winter.

begriffe.erklaerung: The temperature at which water turns into ice: 0 °C.
A tiny, regularly built piece of ice, for example in a snowflake.
A huge, slowly moving mass of ice made of pressed-together snow.
A thin, smooth layer of ice on the ground on which you can easily slip.

gewusst: Freezing water expands so strongly that it can split rocks apart.
In the ice of Antarctica there are trapped air bubbles that are over 800,000 years old and tell researchers about the climate of the past.
The Great Aletsch Glacier is about 20 kilometres long and almost 900 metres thick at its thickest point.

teile.einleitung: Lightning is a gigantic electrical discharge during a thunderstorm. It is hotter than the surface of the Sun and lasts only an instant. If you know how to behave in a thunderstorm, you are well protected.
wichtigste: A flash of lightning heats the air up to about 30,000 degrees.
A flash of lightning lasts less than a second.
Thunder is made because the hot air expands at lightning speed.
In a thunderstorm, get out of the water immediately.
You are fairly safe in a car.
It is dangerous under single trees.
Lightning strikes the tower on the Säntis about 100 times a year.

abschnitte.text: In a thundercloud, ice pellets and water drops whirl around violently. This makes parts of the cloud **electrically** charged. When the voltage becomes too great, it discharges in a flash of **lightning**. It can flash inside the cloud, between clouds or between the cloud and the ground. A flash of lightning lasts only a **fraction of a second**, and sometimes it flickers several times in a row.

A flash of lightning heats the air up to about **30,000 degrees**. That is much hotter than the surface of the Sun. The hot air expands explosively. We hear this as **thunder**. Because light is much faster than sound, you see the lightning first. If you count the seconds until the thunder, about three seconds correspond to one kilometre of distance.

Lightning likes to strike high points. On the **Säntis** in eastern Switzerland there is a tall transmitter tower. Lightning strikes it about **100 times a year**. Researchers have installed measuring instruments there. In this way they learn how strong lightning is and how it happens.

If you are swimming, you must get **out of the water immediately** in a thunderstorm. In the water you are the highest point, and water conducts electricity. In a **car** you are fairly safe. The **metal body** carries the current around the outside into the ground, as long as you do not touch anything metal inside. Buildings with lightning conductors also protect you well.

Never stand under a **single tree** in a thunderstorm. It is often the highest point for a long way around, and lightning likes to strike there. Also avoid hilltops, summits and open fields. Out in the open: crouch down with your feet together and do not lie down on the ground. It is best to look for shelter in good time when a thunderstorm is coming.

gewusst: The lightning conductor was invented in the 18th century by Benjamin Franklin.
Tall towers and mountain peaks are struck by lightning particularly often.

teile.einleitung: Basalt is a dark rock that forms from lava that has hardened. It is the most common volcanic rock on Earth. Even the floor of the oceans and the dark patches on the Moon are made of basalt.
wichtigste: Basalt is usually dark grey to black.
It forms when runny lava cools and hardens.
The floor of the oceans is mostly made of basalt.
Thick flows of basalt often break up into six-sided columns as they cool.
Iceland is mostly built of basalt.
The lunar seas are plains of hardened basalt lava.
Stone wool is made from melted basalt.

abschnitte.text: Basalt is a **volcanic rock**. It forms when lava cools quickly at the Earth's surface. It contains many dark minerals that are rich in **iron** and **magnesium**. That is why it is dark grey to black. Basaltic lava contains little **silica** and is very hot. That is why it is runny and can flow a long way.

At the **mid-ocean ridges**, the Earth's plates are pulling apart. There basaltic lava constantly comes out and hardens in the cold water. This creates the **oceanic crust**, which forms most of the sea floor. The island of **Iceland** lies on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and also on a hotspot. Many volcanic eruptions have built it up from basalt lava.

abschnitte.titel: Columns as if they were built
abschnitte.text: When a thick lava flow cools slowly, it shrinks and cracks. The cracks often form a pattern of mostly **six-sided columns**. The **Giant's Causeway** on the north coast of **Northern Ireland** is famous. There about 40,000 basalt columns stand close together. The place is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The dark areas on the Moon are called **lunar seas**. But there was never any water there. Over three billion years ago, runny lava filled huge impact basins. The dark basalt stands out clearly from the lighter highlands. That is why you can see the lunar seas even with the naked eye.

Basalt is hard and is used for paving stones, crushed stone or floor tiles. Melted at very high temperatures, it can be blown into fine fibres. This makes **stone wool**. This insulating material protects houses against the cold and does not burn.

gewusst: The name Giant's Causeway means a raised path of giants. An old legend tells that a giant built it.
Most of the solid surface of the Earth under the oceans is made of basalt.

teile.einleitung: A dune is a hill of sand piled up by the wind. There are dunes in deserts such as the Sahara, but also on sea coasts such as the North Sea. Some dunes even slowly move along.
wichtigste: Dunes form where the wind drops sand.
The side facing away from the wind is usually steeper.
Moving dunes are slowly pushed along by the wind.
On the North Sea, marram grass holds the sand in place with long roots.
The Dune of Pilat in France is the highest moving dune in Europe.
There are huge fields of dunes in the Sahara.

abschnitte.text: The wind carries grains of sand along with it. Where it becomes weaker, the grains are dropped. Behind a stone or a bush, more and more sand gathers in this way, and a **dune** grows. The wind pushes the sand up the gentle side, the **windward side**. Behind the crest the sand slides down and forms a steep slope, the **leeward side**.

Because the wind keeps blowing sand over the dune, it can slowly move along. It is then called a **moving dune**. Dunes have different shapes. A **crescent dune** is shaped like a half-moon, and its two points face downwind. There are also long dunes that lie in rows like waves. In the **Sahara**, the largest hot desert in the world, dunes form huge seas of sand.

On sea coasts, the wind blows sand inland from the beach. There, plants such as **marram grass** hold the dunes in place. It has very long roots that hold the sand together like a net. Such dunes protect the land from storm floods. That is why you should only walk on the paths: if the plants are trampled, the wind can blow the dune away. The **Dune of Pilat** on the Atlantic coast of France is about 100 metres high.

Some dunes can **hum** or boom. When a lot of sand slides down their steep slope, the grains rub against each other. This creates a deep sound that can be heard far away. They are called **singing dunes**. This sound is known from various deserts around the world.

gewusst: There are also dunes on Mars, which space probes have photographed.
The Dune of Pilat moves a little inland every year, burying trees in the forest behind it.
